analysis.one_liner: Ends tax breaks that reward companies for shifting profits and operations overseas.
analysis.headline: Backed by 117 House Democrats, the bill received no hearing, no vote, and no further committee action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite parts of the 2017 corporate tax law that give special tax breaks to profits U.S. companies book in foreign countries. It would tax foreign profits of U.S.-based companies on the same yearly schedule as domestic profits, take away deductions that reward keeping intangible profits offshore, end a special break for foreign oil and gas income, limit interest deductions for large multinational groups, tighten rules against corporate 'inversions' (relocating headquarters on paper to low-tax countries), and treat foreign companies managed from the United States as domestic for tax purposes [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who would gain revenue as profitable multinationals pay tax on income they currently shelter at reduced rates, plus domestic workers and businesses that compete against companies rewarded for moving profits and operations offshore.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and domestic competitors of multinationals

how_it_helps.text: It repeals deductions for foreign-derived intangible income and global intangible low-taxed income, two categories created by the 2017 tax law that let multinationals pay a reduced rate on profits booked abroad [S2] [S3].
It ends the deemed tax-free return on foreign tangible investments and requires companies to include foreign subsidiary income in the year it is earned, closing timing and rate games [S2] [S3].

It repeals the exclusion of foreign oil and gas extraction income from taxable income of controlled foreign corporations, meaning oil and gas profits booked abroad would no longer be spared [S2] [S3].

It tightens anti-inversion rules by lowering the ownership threshold from 60 percent to 80 percent so companies that shift most ownership abroad are still taxed as domestic, and it treats foreign corporations managed and controlled primarily in the United States as domestic taxpayers [S2] [S3].

It limits the interest deduction for U.S. members of large international financial reporting groups, curbing a technique where debt is loaded onto high-tax jurisdictions to shrink U.S. taxable income [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: U.S.-based multinational corporations and their shareholders, who would pay more tax on foreign profits, foreign oil and gas income, and interest expense, and companies that have inverted or are managed from the U.S. but chartered abroad.

drawbacks.text: U.S.-headquartered companies argue the changes raise their worldwide tax burden relative to foreign competitors who do not pay U.S. tax on similar profits, which supporters of the current rules say is why the 2017 deductions were created [S2] [S3].

The bill applies to tax years beginning after December 31, 2018, reaching into tax years already under way when it was introduced, which businesses criticized as a mid-stream change to the rules they had planned around [S3].

Some provisions are complex: the interest limitation uses companies' own consolidated financial statements under accounting standards to compute tax limits, which adds compliance burden and interpretation questions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill directly targets widely criticized features of the 2017 tax law that reward booking profits offshore, and its main costs fall on a narrow set of large multinationals and their shareholders, though it could modestly disadvantage U.S.-based firms against foreign rivals and adds compliance complexity.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended in January 2021 [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the bill on March 13, 2019, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1] [S5].
117 of the 231 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor is listed [S4].
The House action record shows no activity after the referral — the committee never reported the bill and the full House never considered it [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S. multinational corporations and their shareholders kept the offshore tax breaks the bill would have removed, at no cost to themselves; oil and gas companies kept the foreign extraction income exclusion [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Multinationals kept their offshore tax breaks

for.name: Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 117 cosponsors.

against.name: Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of jurisdiction, never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; the record shows no committee action after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 117 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republicans signed on, and the bill died in a committee chaired by a Democrat without ever reaching the floor [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill removes reduced-rate treatment of foreign profits, the tax-free return on foreign tangible investments, and interest-deduction games, directly raising what profitable multinationals owe [S2] [S3]. Their gain under current law comes from paying less tax than the same income would owe if earned at home.
It repeals the exclusion of foreign oil and gas extraction income from tested income of controlled foreign corporations, ending a carve-out other industries do not get [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: Companies that have inverted or are managed from the U.S. but chartered abroad
industries.note: Tightened anti-inversion rules and a managed-and-controlled test would treat these firms as domestic taxpayers, ending the tax advantage of a paper headquarters move [S2] [S3].
